explanation: Fires on path-like and identifier pieces inside file paths, URLs, include/require statements and header guards: segments such as _html, ruby.exe, /master, /latest, _HPP, the ' <' or ' "' after #include, and ' require' in JS module imports. Ordinary prose tokens get little or no activation.

Fires on the word right after a verb-plus-preposition 'move/route/deliver X to' frame, i.e. the determiner or pronoun that starts the destination ('to[ a] new location', 'to[ its] destination'). It also fires on pointer '*' in C type declarations (T*, struct ip*, BIO *) and on ' PARTICULAR' in 'FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE'. Prepositions or determiners inside scientific prose ('in the', 'of') give weak to moderate activation.

Fires on a word-internal subword fragment that is the start or middle of a longer word being spelled out, e.g. 'AP[PE]ALS' in 'COURT OF APPEALS', 'ant[ip]roliferative', '[se]questration', '[sl]iver', and also on ' of' / ' You' in boilerplate license phrases ('terms of', 'copy of'). Activation is strongest in word-fragment continuations and legal/license boilerplate. Whole common words are weak.

Fires on the first subword fragment of a multi-token Latinate word, especially the prefix fragment 'comp/com/con/extr/intr/dep/prop/impr/disp' at the start of words like compromise, compelling, compulsory, extracellular (also in Portuguese, Spanish and French). The token must be an incomplete word-beginning that needs a continuation. Complete words are weak.

Fires on the token just after a case citation like '37 F.3d 477' (the newline that follows it) and in legal attorney-listing text ('for appellant.', 'with whom'). Elsewhere it gives a moderate-to-strong response on assorted mid-sentence tokens, often connectives or second elements of paired phrases ('and', 'with', 'from', 'Children' after 'Adults/'). There is no clear single trigger outside the legal-citation case.

Fires at boundary or punctuation points in formulaic boilerplate: the street number in the FSF address ('Inc., [5]1 Franklin St'), the ')' in 'CITY (Reuters)', the '.\n\n' after Go BSD license headers, and commas or periods in case captions and company names ('Inc.,'). Scattered other tokens (' log', 'trigger_error', ' cleanser') also fire, so it is a mix centred on templated headers.

Fires on mid-sentence content-word tokens that are fairly rare or specific, mostly proper nouns and compound identifiers: ' Shiite', ' Kurdish', ' TripAdvisor', ' AsyncTask', ' StringBuilder', ' clearTimeout', ' PROCUREMENT' in license text, plus broken CJK byte tokens. There is no clear common semantic thread beyond the token being a distinctive multi-piece word or name.

Fires on syntactic separator or argument positions in code and boilerplate: the token right after an identifier in argument lists or column definitions ('`Feed_ID[`]', 'saveUrl[,]', 'mail($to[,]'), ' express' in 'either express or implied', ' CONTRACT' in 'ACTION OF CONTRACT', and indentation. It is broadly a structured-code/boilerplate position detector with no sharp single trigger.

Fires on the first subword piece after a hyphen or at the start of a word split into pieces, most often an initial 'v' or 'm' fragment ('non-[sm]oking', 'age-[m]atched', '([v]ocals', '[v]igorously', 'N-[m]ethyl', 'shape-[m]aintenance'). The token is a short word-initial consonant fragment that needs a continuation. Strongest for -m/-sm/v pieces after a hyphen or parenthesis.

Fires on the first token of a new statement or clause, i.e. the token right after indentation or a line break in code ('cb', 'alert', 'module', 'SELECT', '[super', ' remove') and the sentence-initial subject or verb in prose ('There[ was]', 'The[ use]', 'We[ affirm]'). It responds to the start of a statement more than to any particular word.

Fires on the token that repeats or closes a previously seen word or pattern: the second occurrence of a repeated noun ('snoring patients', 'supermarket tomatoes', 'bicycle helmet', 'Pride parade'), the ':' after 'Category' in Wikipedia category footers, 'Same as above', and similar list or template continuations. It looks like a copy/repetition detector.

Fires in code snippets at declaration and assignment points: the ' =' after a variable name in 'x = ...' assignments (strongest), the ':' in object-literal keys, and declaration keywords like 'public', 'var', 'class'. Prose tokens are weak.

Fires on the return-type keyword in function or method declarations, mostly ' void' after access modifiers ('private void', 'public static void', '- (void)'), plus 'Sub' in VB, 'case FETCH' and '=' in MATLAB assignments. It also fires on occasional unrelated mid-word fragments in non-English prose. The main job is the function-declaration head.

Fires on second-person or reader-addressing subjects and the modal that follows them in instructions, license text and website notices: ' you' / ' You' in 'you can redistribute', 'By using this site you agree', and ' will' in 'You will find' or 'X will become'. Pronoun subjects such as 'we' and future 'will' fire strongly. Other tokens are weak.
